name: Cyanine Blue
lede: Cyanine blue is an old name that meant a mixed pigment in the nineteenth century and, in Paterson's dictionary, a family of synthetic dyes.

sections.title: Three meanings
sections.body:
*Cyanine* comes from the Greek for blue [1]. The Pigment Compendium records cyanine blue as a nineteenth-century synonym, with Salter (1869) calling it a mixture of [[cobalt-blue]] and [[prussian-blue]] [2]. A similar compound appeared at the time under the name Leitch's blue, and a 1928 source says the pigment was by then obsolete or rarely used [3].

Books disagree on what it was. Some more recent sources imply a phthalocyanine pigment instead of the old mixture [3]. Separately, Paterson describes the cyanines as synthetic dyes, cyanine blue among them, chiefly for photography [1].

The swatch here is a dark blue (lightness 33 on the LCH scale) taken from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, the ISCC-NBS system and Maerz and Paul, with a Ridgway edition of 1886 as the earliest record [4]. Hay's Blue is a near-duplicate, at a CIEDE2000 distance of 2.5 [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Cyanine blue is rare in painting but peaks late. It appears in 81 of 23,781 paintings in our archive, and it is rarer than 53% of the named colors [5]. In the 1900s it is found in 1.1% of the 1,674 paintings from then, about 4.5 times the museums' baseline [5]. As a printed phrase it rose fastest in the 1860s and peaks in the 1910s [6]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [5].
